claim: Mobile zinc is found within glutamatergic vesicles in many excitatory synapses.
source: In many excitatory synapses, mobile zinc is found within glutamatergic vesicles and is coreleased with glutamate.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about synaptic zinc.

claim: Mobile zinc is coreleased with glutamate in many excitatory synapses.
source: In many excitatory synapses, mobile zinc is found within glutamatergic vesicles and is coreleased with glutamate.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about synaptic zinc.

claim: Synaptically released zinc inhibits excitatory neurotransmission at lower frequencies of synaptic activity.
source: Ex vivo studies established that synaptically released (synaptic) zinc inhibits excitatory neurotransmission at lower frequencies of synaptic activity but enhances steady state synaptic responses during higher frequencies of activity.
evidence: This is supported by references to ex vivo studies in the abstract.

claim: Synaptically released zinc enhances steady state synaptic responses during higher frequencies of activity.
source: Ex vivo studies established that synaptically released (synaptic) zinc inhibits excitatory neurotransmission at lower frequencies of synaptic activity but enhances steady state synaptic responses during higher frequencies of activity.
evidence: This is supported by references to ex vivo studies in the abstract.

claim: Synaptic zinc enhanced the gain of sound-evoked responses in CaMKII-expressing principal neurons.
source: We discovered that synaptic zinc enhanced the gain of sound-evoked responses in CaMKII-expressing principal neurons, but it reduced the gain of parvalbumin- and somatostatin-expressing interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Synaptic zinc reduced the gain of parvalbumin-expressing interneurons.
source: We discovered that synaptic zinc enhanced the gain of sound-evoked responses in CaMKII-expressing principal neurons, but it reduced the gain of parvalbumin- and somatostatin-expressing interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Synaptic zinc reduced the gain of somatostatin-expressing interneurons.
source: We discovered that synaptic zinc enhanced the gain of sound-evoked responses in CaMKII-expressing principal neurons, but it reduced the gain of parvalbumin- and somatostatin-expressing interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The modulation by synaptic zinc was sound intensity-dependent.
source: This modulation was sound intensity-dependent and, in part, NMDA receptor-independent.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing differential effects at different sound intensities in Figures 1-5.

claim: The modulation by synaptic zinc was, in part, NMDA receptor-independent.
source: This modulation was sound intensity-dependent and, in part, NMDA receptor-independent.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments with APV shown in Figure 3.

claim: Zinc plays a key role in protein structure, enzymatic catalysis, and cellular regulation as a constituent for nearly 3000 proteins.
source: As a constituent for nearly 3000 proteins, zinc plays a key role in protein structure, enzymatic catalysis, and cellular regulation (Vallee, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vallee, 1988.

claim: Free, mobile zinc is found in secretory tissues such as the prostate, pancreas, and brain.
source: Although the chemistry and biology of zinc metalloproteins have historically dominated the field of zinc biology, there is a growing appreciation for a signaling role of free, mobile zinc found in secretory tissues such as the prostate, pancreas, and especially the brain (Frederickson et al., 2005; Kelleher et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frederickson et al., 2005 and Kelleher et al., 2011.

claim: High concentrations of synaptic zinc are found in glutamatergic excitatory presynaptic vesicles in many brain areas including the neocortex, limbic structures and auditory brainstem.
source: In many brain areas, including the neocortex, limbic structures and auditory brainstem, high concentrations of synaptic zinc are found in glutamatergic excitatory presynaptic vesicles (Frederickson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Frederickson et al., 2005.

claim: More than half of presynaptic glutamatergic terminals in the hippocampus contain synaptic zinc.
source: In the hippocampus, more than half of presynaptic glutamatergic contain synaptic zinc (Sindreu et al., 2003), attesting to zinc's abundance and importance in synaptic function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sindreu et al., 2003.

claim: Synaptic zinc is an inhibitory neuromodulator of AMPA receptors at lower frequencies of synaptic activity.
source: Ex vivo studies established that synaptic zinc is an inhibitory neuromodulator of AMPA receptors, NMDA receptors, and vesicular release probability at lower frequencies of synaptic activity (Kalappa et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2015; Vergnano et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2011; Vogt et al., 2000; Perez-Rosello et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to ex vivo studies.

claim: Synaptic zinc is an inhibitory neuromodulator of NMDA receptors at lower frequencies of synaptic activity.
source: Ex vivo studies established that synaptic zinc is an inhibitory neuromodulator of AMPA receptors, NMDA receptors, and vesicular release probability at lower frequencies of synaptic activity (Kalappa et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2015; Vergnano et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2011; Vogt et al., 2000; Perez-Rosello et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to ex vivo studies.

claim: Synaptic zinc is an inhibitory neuromodulator of vesicular release probability at lower frequencies of synaptic activity.
source: Ex vivo studies established that synaptic zinc is an inhibitory neuromodulator of AMPA receptors, NMDA receptors, and vesicular release probability at lower frequencies of synaptic activity (Kalappa et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2015; Vergnano et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2011; Vogt et al., 2000; Perez-Rosello et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to ex vivo studies.

claim: During higher frequencies of synaptic activity, synaptic zinc inhibits synaptic responses during the first few stimuli but enhances steady state responses during subsequent stimuli.
source: In contrast, during higher frequencies of synaptic activity and during enhanced vesicular release probability, synaptic zinc inhibits synaptic responses during the first few stimuli but enhances steady state responses during subsequent stimuli (Kalappa and Tzounopoulos, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kalappa and Tzounopoulos, 2017.

claim: Low frequency tones (5 or 6 kHz, 40–60 dB SPL) activated two discrete regions of the auditory cortex corresponding to the low frequency regions of A1 and the AAF.
source: Due to the mirror-like reversal of tonotopic gradients between A1 and the anterior auditory field (AAF) (Guo et al., 2012; Joshi et al., 2015), these sounds activated two discrete regions of the auditory cortex corresponding to the low frequency regions of A1 and the AAF (Figure 1a bottom).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1a and citations to Guo et al., 2012 and Joshi et al., 2015.

claim: The response to an 80 dB SPL tone was significantly enhanced after ZX1 application.
source: We observed that the response to an 80 dB SPL tone was significantly enhanced after ZX1 application (Figure 1b,c)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: The response to a 50 dB SPL tone was not affected by ZX1 application.
source: whereas, the response to a 50 dB SPL tone was not affected (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1d,e.

claim: ZX1, but not vehicle, enhanced the amplitude of the fluorescence response for sounds of ≥70 dB SPL.
source: Overall, ZX1, but not vehicle containing ACSF and Alexa-594, enhanced the amplitude of the fluorescence response for sounds of ≥70 dB SPL (Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d,e.

claim: Endogenous extracellular zinc inhibits the gain of sound-evoked A1 responses.
source: These results indicate that endogenous extracellular zinc inhibits the gain of sound-evoked A1 responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the ZX1 enhancement data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Extracellular zinc signaling exerts divisive gain control of sound-evoked A1 responses.
source: By fitting a regression line to this function, we found a slope steeper than unity and no change in the y-intercept (Figure 1g–i), indicating that extracellular zinc signaling exerts divisive gain control of sound-evoked A1 responses.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 1g-i.

claim: ZnT3 KO mice showed larger responses to sounds of 80 dB SPL compared to WT mice.
source: Compared to WT mice, ZnT3 KO mice showed larger responses to sounds of 80 dB SPL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f), suggesting that synaptic zinc inhibits the gain of A1 responses.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Synaptic zinc inhibits the gain of A1 responses.
source: Compared to WT mice, ZnT3 KO mice showed larger responses to sounds of 80 dB SPL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f), suggesting that synaptic zinc inhibits the gain of A1 responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between WT and ZnT3 KO mice.

claim: Zinc chelation in ZnT3 KO mice had no effect on the gain of A1 responses.
source: Moreover, zinc chelation in KO mice had no effect on the gain of A1 responses (Figure 1j–m, Materials and methods), suggesting that, in WT mice, ZX1 enhances A1 gain via chelation of extracellular, ZnT3-dependent zinc.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1j-m.

claim: In WT mice, ZX1 enhances A1 gain via chelation of extracellular, ZnT3-dependent zinc.
source: Moreover, zinc chelation in KO mice had no effect on the gain of A1 responses (Figure 1j–m, Materials and methods), suggesting that, in WT mice, ZX1 enhances A1 gain via chelation of extracellular, ZnT3-dependent zinc.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of ZX1 effects in ZnT3 KO mice.

claim: Extracellular tonic zinc levels in brain slices are ZnT3-independent.
source: Finally, because extracellular tonic, not synaptically-evoked, zinc levels in brain slices are ZnT3-independent (Anderson et al., 2015), our results suggest that synaptically released zinc modulates the gain of sound-evoked responses in A1.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 2015.

claim: Synaptically released zinc modulates the gain of sound-evoked responses in A1.
source: Finally, because extracellular tonic, not synaptically-evoked, zinc levels in brain slices are ZnT3-independent (Anderson et al., 2015), our results suggest that synaptically released zinc modulates the gain of sound-evoked responses in A1.
evidence: This is inferred from the ZnT3-dependence of the ZX1 effects and the ZnT3-independence of tonic zinc.

claim: ZX1 reduced the amplitude of sound-evoked responses of principal neurons to sounds of 60–80 dB SPL.
source: ZX1 reduced the amplitude of sound-evoked responses of principal neurons to sounds of 60–80 dB SPL (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Extracellular zinc signaling exerts multiplicative gain control of the sound-evoked A1 responses in principal neurons.
source: Linear regression analysis showed that the ZX1-induced reduction in the gain was due to a slope shallower than unity (Figure 2c), indicating that extracellular zinc signaling exerts multiplicative gain control of the sound-evoked A1 responses in principal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The effects of synaptic zinc are intensity- and cell type-specific.
source: In contrast to the enhancing effects of ZX1 on responses to sounds of 70–80 dB SPL in all neurons (Figure 1f), the divisive effect of ZX1 on responses to sounds of 60–80 dB SPL in principal neurons suggests that the effects of synaptic zinc are intensity- and cell type-specific.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the effects of ZX1 on all neurons versus principal neurons at different sound intensities.

claim: ZX1 had no effect on the sound-evoked responses of principal neurons in ZnT3 KO mice.
source: ZX1 had no effect on the sound-evoked responses of principal neurons in ZnT3 KO mice, indicating that synaptic zinc increases the gain of principal neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: Synaptic zinc increases the gain of principal neurons.
source: ZX1 had no effect on the sound-evoked responses of principal neurons in ZnT3 KO mice, indicating that synaptic zinc increases the gain of principal neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of ZX1 effects in ZnT3 KO mice.

claim: The sound-evoked responses of principal neurons in A1 are suppressed by inhibitory inputs from parvalbumin-expressing interneurons.
source: Since the sound-evoked responses of principal neurons in A1 are suppressed by inhibitory inputs from parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PV neurons; Li et al., 2013; Seybold et al., 2015; Phillips and Hasenstaub, 2016; Resnik and Polley, 2017), a ZX1-induced increase of the sound-evoked responses of PV neurons would be consistent with the ZX1-induced decrease of the sound-evoked responses observed in principal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: ZX1 increased the sound-evoked responses of PV neurons to all tested sound intensities (30–80 dB SPL).
source: ZX1 increased the sound-evoked responses of PV neurons to all tested sound intensities (30–80 dB SPL, Figure 2d,e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2d,e.

claim: Extracellular zinc exerts divisive gain control of sound-evoked responses in PV neurons.
source: Linear regression analysis showed that the ZX1-induced increase in response gain was due to a slope steeper than unity (Figure 2f), indicating that extracellular zinc exerts divisive gain control of sound-evoked responses in PV neurons.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The enhancing effect of ZX1 on sound-evoked responses of PV neurons was largest for sounds of 60–80 dB SPL.
source: In PV neurons, the enhancing effect of ZX1 on sound-evoked responses was largest for sounds of 60–80 dB SPL (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d) – the intensities where principal neurons showed a ZX1-induced reduction in their responses (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The coupling between the ZX1-induced enhancement in the gain of PV neurons and the ZX1-induced reduction in the gain of principal neurons is consistent with the notion that synaptic zinc increases the gain of principal neurons by decreasing the gain of PV neurons.
source: Although our approach involving the bulk application of ZX1 is not conclusive for distinguishing cell- (direct) vs. circuit-dependent effects (see Discussion for details), this coupling between the ZX1-induced enhancement in the gain of PV neurons (Figure 2ef) and the ZX1-induced reduction in the gain of principal neurons (Figure 2bc) is consistent with the notion that synaptic zinc increases, at least in part, the gain of principal neurons by decreasing the gain of PV neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlated effects of ZX1 on PV and principal neurons.

claim: ZX1 increased the sound-evoked responses of SOM neurons to sounds of lower intensities (30–60 dB SPL).
source: ZX1 increased the sound-evoked responses of SOM neurons to sounds of lower intensities (30–60 dB SPL, Figure 2gh, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d), and increased the gain of these neurons through a positive shift in the y-intercept (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2g,h and Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Extracellular zinc exerts subtractive gain control of sound-evoked A1 responses in SOM neurons.
source: ZX1 increased the sound-evoked responses of SOM neurons to sounds of lower intensities (30–60 dB SPL, Figure 2gh, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d), and increased the gain of these neurons through a positive shift in the y-intercept (Figure 2i). These results support that extracellular zinc exerts subtractive gain control of sound-evoked A1 responses in SOM neurons.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis showing a positive y-intercept shift in Figure 2i.

claim: ZX1 increased the responses of VIP neurons to sounds of 60–80 dB SPL but did not affect their overall response gain.
source: ZX1 increased the responses of VIP neurons to sounds of 60–80 dB SPL but did not affect their overall response gain (Figure 2j–l).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2j-l.

claim: Synaptic zinc is a novel modulator of cortical sound processing that increases the gain of principal neurons, but reduces the gain of PV and SOM neurons.
source: Although the lack of ZX1 effects on the gain of VIP neurons may reflect either a circuit-based cancellation of opposing effects or no direct effect (see Discussion for more details), together, our results show that synaptic zinc is a novel modulator of cortical sound processing – a modulator that increases the gain of principal neurons, but reduces the gain of PV and SOM neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Nanomolar levels of zinc inhibit NMDA receptors.
source: Because nanomolar levels of zinc inhibit NMDA receptors (NMDARs; Paoletti et al., 1997; Hansen et al., 2014), we tested whether NMDARs contribute to the observed zinc-mediated gain modulation in A1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Paoletti et al., 1997 and Hansen et al., 2014.

claim: In the presence of APV, ZX1 increased the responses of principal neurons to sounds of 70–80 dB SPL.
source: In the presence of APV (control), ZX1 increased the responses of principal neurons to sounds of 70–80 dB SPL (Figure 3ab), which is a reversal of the observed ZX1-induced reduction in the sound-evoked responses in the absence of APV (Figure 2ab).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: APV enhanced the sound-evoked responses of principal neurons.
source: Moreover, APV enhanced the sound-evoked responses of principal neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1ab), suggesting that APV disinhibits principal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: APV disinhibits principal neurons.
source: Moreover, APV enhanced the sound-evoked responses of principal neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1ab), suggesting that APV disinhibits principal neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the APV-induced enhancement of principal neuron responses.

claim: In the presence of APV, zinc chelation caused an increase in the sound-evoked responses of PV neurons to sound intensities of 30–80 dB SPL.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, in the presence of APV, zinc chelation caused an increase in the sound-evoked responses of PV neurons to sound intensities of 30–80 dB SPL (Figure 3a,c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a,c.

claim: The disinhibition of principal neurons in the presence of APV unmasked the NMDAR-independent inhibitory effects of zinc on the sound-evoked responses of principal neurons.
source: These results suggest that the disinhibition of principal neurons, in the presence of APV, unmasked the NMDAR-independent inhibitory effects of zinc on the sound-evoked responses of principal neurons, which are likely direct and non-circuit-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from the reversal of ZX1 effects on principal neurons in the presence of APV.

claim: The ZX1-induced increases in the sound-evoked responses of PV neurons in the presence of APV were not different from the increases observed in the absence of APV.
source: The ZX1-induced increases in the sound-evoked responses of PV neurons in the presence of APV (Figure 3c) were not different from the increases observed in the absence of APV (Figure 2f), suggesting that the effects of zinc on the responses of PV neurons are, at least in part, NMDAR-independent.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the ZX1 effects on PV neurons with and without APV.

claim: The effects of zinc on the responses of PV neurons are, at least in part, NMDAR-independent.
source: The ZX1-induced increases in the sound-evoked responses of PV neurons in the presence of APV (Figure 3c) were not different from the increases observed in the absence of APV (Figure 2f), suggesting that the effects of zinc on the responses of PV neurons are, at least in part, NMDAR-independent.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of difference in ZX1 effects on PV neurons with and without APV.

claim: APV reduced the sound-evoked responses of SOM neurons.
source: APV reduced the sound-evoked responses of SOM neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1ef) and abolished the effects of zinc chelation on the sound-evoked responses of SOM neurons (Figure 3d,e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e,f.

claim: APV abolished the effects of zinc chelation on the sound-evoked responses of SOM neurons.
source: APV reduced the sound-evoked responses of SOM neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1ef) and abolished the effects of zinc chelation on the sound-evoked responses of SOM neurons (Figure 3d,e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3d,e.

claim: The effects of synaptic zinc on the sound-evoked responses of SOM neurons are NMDAR-dependent.
source: Although potential circuit effects due to NMDAR-dependent and NMDAR-independent effects that cancel each other out can't be ruled out (see Discussion for more details), our results are consistent with the notion that the effects of synaptic zinc on the sound-evoked responses of SOM neurons are NMDAR-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from the abolishment of ZX1 effects on SOM neurons by APV.

claim: APV enhanced the sound-evoked responses of VIP neurons.
source: APV enhanced the sound-evoked responses of VIP neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1gh) and abolished the effects of ZX1 on the sound-evoked responses of VIP neurons (Figure 3df), suggesting that synaptic zinc inhibits the sound-evoked responses of VIP neurons, likely, via NMDAR-dependent mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1g,h.

claim: APV abolished the effects of ZX1 on the sound-evoked responses of VIP neurons.
source: APV enhanced the sound-evoked responses of VIP neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1gh) and abolished the effects of ZX1 on the sound-evoked responses of VIP neurons (Figure 3df), suggesting that synaptic zinc inhibits the sound-evoked responses of VIP neurons, likely, via NMDAR-dependent mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3d,f.

claim: Synaptic zinc inhibits the sound-evoked responses of VIP neurons, likely via NMDAR-dependent mechanisms.
source: APV enhanced the sound-evoked responses of VIP neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1gh) and abolished the effects of ZX1 on the sound-evoked responses of VIP neurons (Figure 3df), suggesting that synaptic zinc inhibits the sound-evoked responses of VIP neurons, likely, via NMDAR-dependent mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the abolishment of ZX1 effects on VIP neurons by APV.

claim: Synaptic zinc modulates non-NMDAR targets to inhibit the gain of sound-evoked responses of principal and PV neurons.
source: Overall, our results highlight that synaptic zinc modulates non-NMDAR targets to inhibit the gain of sound-evoked responses of principal and PV neurons; and suggest that NMDAR-mediated signaling is involved in the zinc-mediated gain control of SOM and VIP neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMDAR-independent effects of zinc on principal and PV neurons.

claim: NMDAR-mediated signaling is involved in the zinc-mediated gain control of SOM and VIP neurons.
source: Overall, our results highlight that synaptic zinc modulates non-NMDAR targets to inhibit the gain of sound-evoked responses of principal and PV neurons; and suggest that NMDAR-mediated signaling is involved in the zinc-mediated gain control of SOM and VIP neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMDAR-dependent effects of zinc on SOM and VIP neurons.

claim: ZX1 reduced the responses of individual L2/3 principal neurons to sounds of 70 dB SPL.
source: ZX1 reduced the responses to sounds of 70 dB SPL (Figure 4b,c), and linear regression analysis showed that this reduction in gain was divisive (Figure 4d), which is consistent with our results obtained with transcranial imaging (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4b,c.

claim: The reduction in gain of individual L2/3 principal neurons by ZX1 was divisive.
source: ZX1 reduced the responses to sounds of 70 dB SPL (Figure 4b,c), and linear regression analysis showed that this reduction in gain was divisive (Figure 4d), which is consistent with our results obtained with transcranial imaging (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Synaptic zinc exerts multiplicative gain control of sound-evoked responses in individual L2/3 principal neurons.
source: These results show that synaptic zinc exerts multiplicative gain control of sound-evoked responses in individual L2/3 principal neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the divisive gain change observed in individual L2/3 principal neurons.

claim: Individual L2/3 PV neurons showed increased sound-evoked responses to sounds of 50 and 70 dB SPL after ZX1 application.
source: PV neurons showed increased sound-evoked responses to sounds of 50 and 70 dB SPL (Figure 4f,g) and a multiplicative increase in their gain (Figure 4h), suggesting that synaptic zinc exerts divisive gain control of sound-evoked responses in individual L2/3 PV neurons.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4f,g.

claim: Synaptic zinc exerts divisive gain control of sound-evoked responses in individual L2/3 PV neurons.
source: PV neurons showed increased sound-evoked responses to sounds of 50 and 70 dB SPL (Figure 4f,g) and a multiplicative increase in their gain (Figure 4h), suggesting that synaptic zinc exerts divisive gain control of sound-evoked responses in individual L2/3 PV neurons.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis showing a multiplicative gain increase in Figure 4h.

claim: ZX1 caused an additive gain increase in individual L2/3 SOM neurons.
source: We performed similar two-photon experiments in individual L2/3 SOM and VIP neurons (Figure 5) and the results we obtained were, overall, consistent with the results we observed with transcranial imaging: ZX1 caused an additive gain increase in L2/3 SOM neurons (Figure 5a–d) and no significant changes in the gain of L2/3 VIP neurons (Figure 5e–h).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5a-d.

claim: ZX1 caused no significant changes in the gain of individual L2/3 VIP neurons.
source: We performed similar two-photon experiments in individual L2/3 SOM and VIP neurons (Figure 5) and the results we obtained were, overall, consistent with the results we observed with transcranial imaging: ZX1 caused an additive gain increase in L2/3 SOM neurons (Figure 5a–d) and no significant changes in the gain of L2/3 VIP neurons (Figure 5e–h).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5e-h.

claim: Synaptic zinc increases the gain of principal neurons, but decreases the gain of PV and SOM interneurons in individual L2/3 neurons.
source: Together, our two-photon experiments on individual L2/3 neurons support the cell-specific effect of synaptic zinc on A1 neurons: synaptic zinc increases the gain of principal neurons, but decreases the gain of PV and SOM interneurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the two-photon imaging findings supported by data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Gain modulation provides a mechanism for generating sensory representations that are robust to noise.
source: Therefore, gain modulation provides a mechanism for generating sensory representations that are robust to noise, thus maximizing sensitivity to changes in stimulus intensity across variable auditory contexts.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about gain modulation in sensory systems.

claim: Gain modulation maintains the robustness of central responses after peripheral damage.
source: Moreover, gain modulation maintains the robustness of central responses after peripheral damage.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about gain modulation in sensory systems.

claim: Sensory experience alters synaptic zinc levels in primary somatosensory and visual cortex.
source: Sensory experience alters synaptic zinc levels in primary somatosensory and visual cortex (Brown and Dyck, 2002; Dyck et al., 2003); however, the physiological roles of this plasticity in sensory processing remain unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown and Dyck, 2002 and Dyck et al., 2003.

claim: Sound-dependent changes in zinc signaling have been demonstrated in the dorsal cochlear nucleus.
source: Based on our results, we propose that sound-dependent changes in zinc signaling, which have been demonstrated in the dorsal cochlear nucleus (Kalappa et al., 2015), may contribute to the activity-dependent changes in cortical gain.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kalappa et al., 2015.

claim: Synaptic zinc is present in many cortical areas.
source: Synaptic zinc is present in many cortical areas (Danscher and Stoltenberg, 2005) and dynamic gain modulation is a fundamental mechanism across many brain regions affecting sensory computations, attention, multisensory integration and value estimation (Somers et al., 1995; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009; Ohshiro et al., 2011; Louie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Danscher and Stoltenberg, 2005.

claim: Dynamic gain modulation is a fundamental mechanism across many brain regions affecting sensory computations, attention, multisensory integration and value estimation.
source: Synaptic zinc is present in many cortical areas (Danscher and Stoltenberg, 2005) and dynamic gain modulation is a fundamental mechanism across many brain regions affecting sensory computations, attention, multisensory integration and value estimation (Somers et al., 1995; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009; Ohshiro et al., 2011; Louie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Gain modulation is mediated by selective increases or decreases in cortical inhibition.
source: Gain modulation is mediated by selective increases or decreases in cortical inhibition (Li et al., 2013; Olsen et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012; Phillips and Hasenstaub, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: PV neurons provide multiplicative/divisive gain control of principal neurons.
source: Recent studies, including optogenetic approaches to increase the activity of PV and SOM neurons, have suggested that PV neurons provide multiplicative/divisive gain control of principal neurons, whereas SOM neurons provide additive/subtractive gain control of principal neurons (Atallah et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 2012; Moore and Wehr, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: SOM neurons provide additive/subtractive gain control of principal neurons.
source: Recent studies, including optogenetic approaches to increase the activity of PV and SOM neurons, have suggested that PV neurons provide multiplicative/divisive gain control of principal neurons, whereas SOM neurons provide additive/subtractive gain control of principal neurons (Atallah et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 2012; Moore and Wehr, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation and inactivation of PV and SOM neurons revealed asymmetric effects on neuronal gain in auditory cortex.
source: However, activation and inactivation of PV and SOM neurons revealed asymmetric effects on neuronal gain in auditory cortex (Phillips and Hasenstaub, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Phillips and Hasenstaub, 2016.

claim: The results are consistent with the role of PV neurons in providing dynamic gain control in A1.
source: Therefore, our results are consistent with the role of PV neurons in providing dynamic gain control in A1 and add zinc as a player in the gain control of L2/3 cortical circuits.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed zinc-mediated effects on PV neurons and principal neurons.

claim: VIP neurons provide inhibition to both SOM and PV neurons.
source: Since VIP neurons provide inhibition to both SOM and PV neurons (Pi et al., 2013; Harris and Shepherd, 2015), these findings suggest that synaptic zinc modulates the VIP-mediated disinhibition of SOM and PV neurons, which, in turn, shape the gain of principal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pi et al., 2013 and Harris and Shepherd, 2015.

claim: Synaptic zinc modulates the VIP-mediated disinhibition of SOM and PV neurons, which shape the gain of principal neurons.
source: Since VIP neurons provide inhibition to both SOM and PV neurons (Pi et al., 2013; Harris and Shepherd, 2015), these findings suggest that synaptic zinc modulates the VIP-mediated disinhibition of SOM and PV neurons, which, in turn, shape the gain of principal neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed effects of zinc on VIP, SOM, PV, and principal neurons.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of NMDARs reduced the spontaneous firing rates of PV neurons in the prefrontal cortex.
source: Similarly, in the prefrontal cortex pharmacological blockade of NMDARs reduced the spontaneous firing rates of PV neurons and increased the spontaneous firing rates of principal neurons (Homayoun and Moghaddam, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Homayoun and Moghaddam, 2007.

claim: Synaptic zinc fine-tunes excitatory synaptic transmission and sensory processing.
source: Together, our results and previous findings on the role of zinc in modulating glutamatergic neurotransmission demonstrate that synaptic zinc fine-tunes excitatory synaptic transmission and sensory processing.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the current results and previous findings.

claim: Zinc fine-tuning does not impair baseline neurotransmission or basic sensory and sensorimotor functions, such as hearing thresholds and prepulse inhibition.
source: Although this fine-tuning does not impair baseline neurotransmission or basic sensory and sensorimotor functions, such as hearing thresholds and prepulse inhibition (Cole et al., 2001; Thackray et al., 2017), it has profound consequences on synaptic plasticity (Pan et al., 2011), sound-evoked cortical processing and more intricate, yet ethologically crucial sensory processing tasks, such as gain modulation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cole et al., 2001 and Thackray et al., 2017.
